server: prefect server start, official image, against postgres:16

plain_process.where: plain python process in the prefect image, box idle, taken before the runs

plain_process_after_runs.where: plain python process in the prefect image, taken after the runs

fibo31_measurements.canonical_source: median of the three uncontended plain-process measurements taken on the idle box; this is the figure used for every ceiling percentage
fibo31_measurements.spread_note: The body is 0.111s uncontended and up to 0.125s when measured inside a single @task thread or a pool subprocess (interpreter warm-up and one-off scheduling noise, each measured once rather than in a loop). Using the slowest figure the ceiling would be 160.1 units/s instead of 180.0, which moves in_process cpu from 4.7% to 5.2% of ceiling and changes no conclusion.

cpu.sensitivity: using the slowest body measurement (0.1249s) the ceiling would be 160.1/s instead of 180.0/s

in_process.mechanism: ThreadPoolTaskRunner(max_workers=20); 2000 @task .submit() calls in one flow run, executed as threads of the flow process
in_process.unit_isolation: none - all 2000 units share one CPython process and its GIL

work_pool.mechanism: process work pool 'bench', pool concurrency limit 20, one prefect worker; 2000 deployment runs, each executed as its own subprocess

work_pool_tuned.mechanism: same as work_pool with the worker poll loop at 0.1s

settings_changed_from_default.default: None, which resolves to sys.maxsize (one thread per submitted task)
settings_changed_from_default.why: the experiment fixes concurrency at 20; Prefect's own default would spawn 2000 threads
the 10s default caps the dispatch rate at one pool-worth (20 runs) per 10s

settings_changed_from_default.used: not used - run_deployment is never called; the 2000 runs are created directly with PrefectClient.create_flow_run_from_deployment so that submission is not the bottleneck
settings_changed_from_default.why: run_deployment blocks waiting for its own run, which would serialise submission

settings_changed_from_default.default: DEFAULT (inputs + task source), inert unless results are persisted
settings_changed_from_default.why: 2000 identical calls must not be served from cache
20 concurrent subprocesses plus the server's pools exhaust 100
the box has 123 GiB and the default starves the server

settings_left_at_default.value: unset; bounded by the pool's concurrency limit of 20

settings_left_at_default.setting: task runner for the in_process configuration

measurement.source: Prefect's own database: task_run_state for in_process, flow_run_state for the work pool configurations. No harness clock is used for any reported figure.
measurement.throughput: jobs / (max COMPLETED timestamp - min RUNNING timestamp)
measurement.latency: COMPLETED timestamp - submission timestamp, p50 and p95
measurement.submission_anchor_in_process: the uuid7 task run id minted by ThreadPoolTaskRunner.submit(); task_run.created is unusable because the server's task-run recorder inserts the row tens of seconds after the run
measurement.cpu_accounting: host-wide /proc/stat sampled once a second, sliced to each rep's measured window; for in_process also getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF) of the flow process itself
measurement.reps: 1 warmup discarded, then 5 measured, per configuration and workload

batch_sizes.note: Batch sizes differ per configuration. Throughput is reported as units/second in every case, so the figures are comparable, but the runs are not equal-sized. The poll-bound work-pool configurations run at a stable rate, so a smaller batch measures that rate in a fraction of the time; in_process sleep is capped at 500 by the event-broker finding below.

event_broker_overflow.summary: A single-node Prefect server silently loses its own task-run records once in-process task throughput exceeds what the task-run recorder can drain. Above that rate the server's database is an incomplete record of what ran.
event_broker_overflow.mechanism: In-process @task state changes are not written by synchronous API calls. The task engine emits events, the server's in-memory broker queues them, and a task_run_recorder service consumes the queue and inserts task_run and task_run_state rows. The broker's per-subscription queue is a hardcoded asyncio.Queue(maxsize=10000) in prefect/server/utilities/messaging/memory.py (line 113, Prefect 3.8.6); there is no setting that raises it. When it fills, the broker discards the message.
event_broker_overflow.log_line: server-1  | 16:01:22.874 | WARNING | prefect.server.utilities.messaging.memory - Subscription queue is full, dropping message for topic='events' queue_size=10000 retry_queue_size=0
event_broker_overflow.silent: The only signal is that WARNING in the server's own log. The client reports success, every flow run finishes COMPLETED, the flow's futures all resolve, and nothing in the API or the UI indicates that records are missing. A consumer reading task_run / task_run_state sees fewer units than ran, with no error.

observed_loss.setup: six back-to-back in_process sleep reps of 2000 @task units each, 20-way, roughly 15s per rep, about 130 task/s
observed_loss.first_drop: 16:01:22.874, 13.9s into rep 2, i.e. after roughly 2.5 reps (about 5000 task runs) had been produced
observed_loss.note: Rows that were recorded can also be incomplete: rep 3 recorded 973 task runs but only 725 of them with a COMPLETED state, so both the run and its state history can go missing.

event_broker_overflow.rate_at_which_dropping_starts: The recorder persists task runs at roughly 30.5 per second while the flow process is competing for the box and about 59.4 per second once it has the box to itself. The in_process configuration produces them at about 150 units/s on the sleep body, two to five times faster. The broker's 10000-message queue absorbs the first burst, which is why the first one or two reps come out intact, but any run that sustains more than roughly 59.4 task runs/s fills the queue and the server begins discarding its own records. In this probe 1000 of 6000 task runs were never written, and the recorder needed 61.9s after the last rep finished to persist what it had kept.

drain_measurement.experiment: three back-to-back 2000-unit in_process sleep reps with no drain barrier, 20-way, while sampling once a second how many task_run rows the server had persisted for those reps
drain_measurement.first_drop_line: server-1  | 17:08:05.429 | WARNING | prefect.server.utilities.messaging.memory - Subscription queue is full, dropping message for topic='events' queue_size=10000 retry_queue_size=0
drain_measurement.conclusion: The recorder persists task runs at roughly 30.5 per second while the flow process is competing for the box and about 59.4 per second once it has the box to itself. The in_process configuration produces them at about 150 units/s on the sleep body, two to five times faster. The broker's 10000-message queue absorbs the first burst, which is why the first one or two reps come out intact, but any run that sustains more than roughly 59.4 task runs/s fills the queue and the server begins discarding its own records. In this probe 1000 of 6000 task runs were never written, and the recorder needed 61.9s after the last rep finished to persist what it had kept.

event_broker_overflow.consequence_for_this_benchmark: in_process sleep had to be measured at 500 units per rep instead of 2000. At 500 all six reps recorded 500/500 and no drop warnings were logged. in_process cpu runs at 8.4 units/s, two orders of magnitude below the drain limit, so its 2000-unit reps all recorded 2000/2000 and were kept.

gil_bound_in_process_cpu.summary: The in_process configuration nominally spreads 20-way, but on a CPU-bound body it uses 1.03 cores, 5.1% of the 20 it spans, and reaches 8.39 units/s against a 180.0 units/s ceiling, 4.7% of it. The 20 'concurrent' tasks are threads of one CPython process, so the GIL serialises them.
gil_bound_in_process_cpu.why: ThreadPoolTaskRunner runs each @task in a thread of the flow's own process. Nothing is dispatched and nothing is isolated, so 20-way concurrency buys overlap only where the body releases the GIL. time.sleep does; a naive recursive fibo does not.

how_the_core_figure_was_taken.primary: resource.getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF) in the flow process, read immediately before the flow call and immediately after it returns. ru_utime + ru_stime deltas give the CPU-seconds the process consumed; dividing by the wall seconds of the same interval gives cores busy. RUSAGE_SELF covers every thread of the process, and in this configuration all 2000 task bodies are threads of it, so nothing escapes the accounting.
how_the_core_figure_was_taken.cross_check: host-wide /proc/stat sampled once a second and sliced to each rep's measured window, which gives the flow process plus the Prefect server and Postgres
how_the_core_figure_was_taken.box: 32 vCPU, nothing else running on it

gil_bound_in_process_cpu.contrast_with_sleep_workload: On the sleep body the same configuration reaches far higher throughput, because time.sleep releases the GIL and 20 threads do overlap. The gap between the two workloads in this one configuration is the GIL, not Prefect's orchestration.
